title: Multiple sclerosis: damaged wiring, extra work
description: In multiple sclerosis the immune system damages the insulation of nerve fibres, and over time the fibres and grey matter themselves. The episode follows what is seen when a person with MS moves a hand: more of the cortex is active than in someone without MS, and the more damage there is, the more widespread that activity. Researchers think this extra activity may help limit the effect of the damage.
caveat: The damage itself, in the white matter and grey matter, is spread through the brain and is described, not drawn. The activity findings come from one study of 30 people with the primary progressive form of MS, which is less common than the relapsing form, so they may not apply to everyone with MS. That the extra activity is helpful is the researchers' suggestion. A large pooled analysis of brain activity at rest found both stronger and weaker links in these same areas, so the picture depends on what is measured.

phases.name: Damage to the wiring
phases.caption: Patches of inflammation damage the insulation of nerve fibres, and more subtle damage spreads through the white and grey matter. This is spread widely, so it is described, not drawn.

phases.name: Moving a hand
phases.caption: When the person moves their hand, more of the brain is active than in someone without MS: the supplementary motor area, the insula, and areas in the temporal, parietal and occipital lobes that combine information from different senses.

order.rationale: The movement findings compare people with MS and healthy people at one time point. Placing them after the damage is an inference from the activity being related to the amount of damage.

phases.name: More damage, more spread
phases.caption: The more damage visible on scans, the more widespread this extra activity. Researchers suggest the brain may be recruiting extra areas to limit the effect of the damage.

order.rationale: This is a relationship across people with different amounts of damage, not a change over time in one person.

phases.name: At rest
phases.caption: The hand is still and the extra activity is no longer drawn.

order.rationale: The movement findings apply while moving; returning to rest follows from that.

regions.explanation: More active than in people without MS while moving a hand, in one study of 30 people with primary progressive MS. A pooled analysis of the brain at rest found the right supplementary motor area less connected, so findings differ between activity during movement and connections at rest.

citations.authors: Rocca MA, Matthews PM, Caputo D, Ghezzi A, Falini A, Scotti G, Comi G, Filippi M
citations.title: Evidence for widespread movement-associated functional MRI changes in patients with PPMS.
citations.quote: Compared with control subjects, patients with MS showed increased activation of brain regions within both traditional motor planning and execution regions (including the supplementary motor area and the cingulate motor area), the insula (a region implicated in sensory processing), and several multimodal cortical regions in the temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes.

citations.authors: Rocca MA, Matthews PM, Caputo D, Ghezzi A, Falini A, Scotti G, Comi G, Filippi M
citations.title: Evidence for widespread movement-associated functional MRI changes in patients with PPMS.
citations.quote: fMRI was used to assess patterns of brain activations associated with 3 different motor tasks in 30 right-handed patients with primary progressive MS (PPMS) and variable degrees of motor impairment, which were compared with those from 15 right-handed, sex- and age-matched control subjects.
